newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistanis vote in fourth election in nine years.
newsitem.headline: Pakistanis vote in fourth election in nine years.

text.p: Pakistanis began voting on Monday in an election forced by President Farooq Leghari's dismissal of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto three months ago on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Only a few voters were waiting when polling stations opened at 7:00 a.m. (0200 GMT) in the capital, Islamabad, an hour earlier than usual due to the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.

One young voter, Mohammad Agha, waved a key-ring in the shape of a tiger, electoral symbol of Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League (PML). "That's who I'm going to vote for and so is everyone else," he said before entering the polling booth.
About 56.5 million Pakistanis aged 21 and over are eligible to vote in the elections for a new 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) and four provincial assemblies.
The 36,415 polling stations, tightly guarded by police and 250,000 troops on election duty, will stay open until 4:00 p.m. (1100 GMT), with results expected in the evening.
Officials say 1,758 candidates are vying for seats in the National Assembly and 4,426 for seats in the Punjab, Sindh, North West Frontier and Balochistan provincial assemblies.
The main fight is between the PML, fielding 177 National Assembly candidates, and Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, fielding 161.

Ex-cricketer Imran Khan's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) has put up 132 candidates, a splinter PPP faction led by Bhutto's estranged sister-in-law Ghinwa Bhutto 66, and the Karachi-based ethnic Mohajir National Movement 55. Others are from smaller parties or are standing as independents.
Leghari promised in an address to the nation on Sunday night that the polls would be free, fair and open.
"By tomorrow night, we will...complete the process of free, fair and transparent elections," he declared on television.
Former prime minister Sharif said he was confident of winning. His main rival, Bhutto, fighting for political survival, accused the president of planning to rig the vote.
Opinion polls indicate that Sharif will win, but a spokesman for Bhutto dismissed such surveys as media gimmicks arranged by what he called forces seeking to rig the elections.
Bhutto said she had reports that the caretaker government planned to rig the vote in 63 National Assembly constituencies and she would not accept the result if this happened.
Leghari urged people to vote "wisely and selflessly" to elect representatives who could give a good government.

"Pakistan stands at a crossroads," he said. "We need political leaders with vision and courage to steer this country out of the woods. Corruption, waste and inefficiency have eaten into the vitals of our state."
Chief Election Commissioner Fakhre Alam said on Sunday that he expected a good turn-out -- although there have been clear signs of voter apathy during a lacklustre Ramadan campaign.
